## Prior review verdict

The prior review found the core deliverables (router.tsx, RequireAuth, HomePage, App.tsx/App.test.tsx) fully spec-compliant, and the jsdom→happy-dom bug fix technically sound, BUT found one Important issue: the follow-up report claimed "jsdom removed" when in fact pnpm-lock.yaml still had full jsdom resolution entries and it was still physically in node_modules.

A clean `rm -rf node_modules && pnpm install` from repo root fully dropped jsdom (root cause: pnpm's incremental resolver doesn't drop satisfied-but-now-unused optional peers on `pnpm install`/`pnpm dedupe` alone — needed a full reinstall). This also picked up some unrelated transitive patch-version bumps in server's dependency tree (express-rate-limit/hono/fast-uri/systeminformation). Read the fix details: /Users/taha/Documents/chapters/.superpowers/sdd/task-7-followup-report.md (the "## Fix: fully remove jsdom from lockfile" section at the end).

The controller independently ran the full server test suite (130 tests, real Postgres) after this fix to check the transitive server dependency bumps didn't break anything server-side — confirmed 130/130 passing.

## What to verify now

## Diff Under Review (all 4 commits, full Task 7)

**Base:** 9fe1350
**Head:** f934f35
**Diff file:** /Users/taha/Documents/chapters/.superpowers/sdd/review-9fe1350..f934f35.diff

Read the diff file once. Do not re-run git commands. Do not crawl the broader codebase beyond a concrete named risk. Read-only review.

1. Confirm jsdom is actually gone now: grep the diff/current pnpm-lock.yaml content for "jsdom" — it should show at most vitest's own peerDependencies/peerDependenciesMeta declaration (metadata, not a resolved package), with no `jsdom@29.1.1:` resolution/snapshot block and no entry under any `optionalDependencies:` block pointing to a resolved jsdom package.
2. Confirm client/package.json has no jsdom devDependency.
3. Spot-check that the transitive bumps to server's dependencies (express-rate-limit, hono, fast-uri, systeminformation or similar) are patch/minor version bumps, not anything that looks like a major version jump that would warrant more scrutiny — this project has previously been burned by an unreviewed major-version dependency bump breaking CI (a Dependabot incident), so treat any major-version jump here as worth flagging even though this diff wasn't a deliberate dependency update.

Verify claims against the diff directly.

touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a

every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

150:## Fix: fully remove jsdom from lockfile
151-
152-The prior report above (`## jsdom removal — verification`) was wrong: it
153-claimed `pnpm install`'s `Packages: -1` meant jsdom was gone, but it never
154-grepped `pnpm-lock.yaml` afterward. jsdom was removed from
155-`client/package.json`'s `devDependencies` but the lockfile still carried a
156-full `jsdom@29.1.1` resolution/snapshot, wired in as an `optionalDependency`
157-of the shared `vitest@3.2.7(...)` resolution used by both `client` and
158-`server`. It was also still physically present under `node_modules/.pnpm/`.
159-
160-### Root cause
161-
162-`vitest`'s own `package.json` declares `jsdom: '*'` as an **optional**
163-`peerDependency`. pnpm's default `auto-install-peers=true` (no `.npmrc` in
164-this repo overrides it) auto-resolves optional peers to the latest matching
165-version whenever it can — even when nothing in the workspace actually wants
166-them. Once resolved, pnpm's incremental resolver (used by plain `pnpm
167-install` and even `pnpm dedupe`) treats an already-satisfied optional-peer
168-binding as still valid and keeps reusing it release over release; it doesn't
169-proactively drop a binding just because the last thing that needed it was
170-deleted from `package.json`. That's exactly what happened here: jsdom was a
171-real, used `devDependency` of `client` before Task 7's happy-dom switch;
172-removing it from `package.json` didn't retroactively invalidate the
